questionText: Series: 64,81,100,121,... Which number NOT in series?
hints: Look at what kind of numbers are in the series. Each one comes from multiplying a number by itself.
64 is 8 × 8 and 81 is 9 × 9. Test each choice to see whether it is a number multiplied by itself.
Here is a similar one: the series 1, 4, 9, 16 holds square numbers. 49 belongs, because 7 × 7 = 49. 50 does not belong, because it falls between 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64.

stepByStep.text: The series is 8 × 8, 9 × 9, 10 × 10, 11 × 11. These are square numbers.
169 is 13 × 13, 225 is 15 × 15 and 289 is 17 × 17. They all belong.
13 × 13 = 169 and 14 × 14 = 196. No whole number multiplied by itself gives a number between these two.
176 lies between 169 and 196. So 176 is not in the series.

misconceptions.A: 169 is 13 × 13, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 176 falls between 13 × 13 and 14 × 14, so it is not a square number.
misconceptions.C: 225 is 15 × 15, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.
misconceptions.D: 289 is 17 × 17, so it is in the series. Look for the number that is not a number times itself.

questionText: Sum of series 1,3,5,7,...,27?
hints: These are the odd numbers in order, starting from 1. Sums of odd numbers starting from 1 make a special pattern.
Try small cases first, such as 1 + 3 and 1 + 3 + 5. Then count how many odd numbers there are from 1 to 27.
Here is a similar one: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 has 5 odd numbers and adds up to 25. That is 5 × 5. So the sum of the first 5 odd numbers is (5)².

stepByStep.text: Look at small cases. 1 + 3 = 4, which is 2 × 2. And 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, which is 3 × 3. The sum is always the count of odd numbers multiplied by itself.
Count the odd numbers from 1 to 27. Add 1 to 27 and halve it.
There are 14 odd numbers, so the sum is 14 × 14.
So the sum is (14)².

misconceptions.A: Count the odd numbers again. 27 is the 14th odd number, not the 13th.
misconceptions.B: Yes! There are 14 odd numbers from 1 to 27, so the sum is 14 × 14.
misconceptions.C: Count how many odd numbers there are: (27 + 1) ÷ 2. The sum is that count multiplied by itself.
misconceptions.D: The sum depends on how many odd numbers there are, not on how big the last one is. Count them: (27 + 1) ÷ 2.

questionText: A man walked a total of 66 km in 6 days. Every day he walked 4 km less than the previous day. How many kilometer did he walk on the 6th day?
hints: The distance goes down by the same amount every day, so the last day is the shortest. Compare each of the other days with the last day and see how much extra was walked.
Day 5 was 4 km more than day 6, and day 4 was 8 km more than day 6. Carry on back to day 1 and add up all these extra kilometres.

Here is a similar one. A girl reads 30 pages in 3 days, reading 2 pages fewer each day. Compared with day 3, she read 4 extra pages on day 1 and 2 extra on day 2, which is 6 extra. 30 − 6 = 24 and 24 ÷ 3 = 8, so she read 8 pages on day 3.

stepByStep.text: Compare each day with day 6. Days 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 were 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 km longer than day 6.
Add up the extra kilometres. They come to 60 km.
Take the extra away from the total. What is left is 6 walks, each as long as the walk on day 6.
Share 6 km equally over 6 days to get 1 km a day. As a check, 21 + 17 + 13 + 9 + 5 + 1 = 66. He walked 1 km on the 6th day.

misconceptions.A: If the last day were 3 km, the six days would be 23, 19, 15, 11, 7 and 3 km, which add up to 78 km. That is more than 66 km, so the last day must be shorter.
misconceptions.B: If the last day were 2 km, the six days would be 22, 18, 14, 10, 6 and 2 km, which add up to 72 km. That is more than 66 km, so the last day must be shorter.
misconceptions.C: 11 km is 66 ÷ 6, the average for one day. The last day is the shortest day, so it must be less than the average.
misconceptions.D: Well done! The days were 21, 17, 13, 9, 5 and 1 km, which add up to 66 km, so the 6th day was 1 km.

questionText: How many terms are there in the sequence: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, ............ 113?
hints: The numbers go up by the same amount each time. Count how many jumps it takes to get from the first number to the last, and remember that there is one more number than there are jumps.

Here is a similar one: 2, 5, 8 and so on up to 32. Each jump is 3, and from 2 to 32 is 30. 30 ÷ 3 = 10 jumps, and 10 jumps join 11 numbers, so there are 11 terms.

From the first number to the last is a distance of 112.
Count the jumps of 7 in 112. There are 16 jumps.
Jumps sit between numbers, so 16 jumps join 17 numbers. The first number is there before any jump, which is easy to forget. There are 17 terms.

misconceptions.B: Great job! There are 16 jumps of 7 from 1 to 113, and 16 jumps join 17 terms.
misconceptions.C: 16 is the number of jumps of 7. There is one more number than there are jumps, because the first number is there before any jump.
misconceptions.D: 6 is far too few for a list that reaches 113. Find how many jumps of 7 fit between 1 and 113, then add 1.

questionText: The 10th term of the series: 24, 39, 53, 66, 78, ............

Five terms are given, so 78 is the 5th term. Five more jumps are needed to reach the 10th term: 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7.

The 9th term is 108 + 8 = 116. The 10th term is 116 + 7, which is 123.

misconceptions.C: 108 is the 8th term. Keep going for two more jumps to reach the 10th term.
misconceptions.D: 118 is close. Check the jumps after 78, which are 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7, and add them one at a time.

questionText: What comes next: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ______

Here is a similar one: 0, 3, 8, 15. The jumps are 3, 5 and 7, the odd numbers in order. The next jump is 9, so the next number is 15 + 9 = 24.

stepByStep.text: Each number is a counting number multiplied by itself: 1 × 1 = 1, 2 × 2 = 4, 3 × 3 = 9, 4 × 4 = 16 and 5 × 5 = 25.
The next one uses 6. 6 times 6 is 36, so the next number is 36.

misconceptions.A: Excellent thinking! The numbers are 1 × 1, 2 × 2 and so on, and 6 × 6 = 36.
misconceptions.B: 49 is 7 × 7, which skips one. After 5 × 5 comes 6 × 6.
misconceptions.C: 35 is 25 + 10. The jumps here are 3, 5, 7 and 9, so the next jump is 11.
misconceptions.D: 30 is 5 × 6. In this pattern each number is multiplied by itself, so use 6 × 6.

hints: Look at the jumps between the numbers. If the jumps are not all the same, look for a pattern in the jumps themselves.
Work out the jumps from 1 to 3, from 3 to 6, from 6 to 10 and so on. See how much each jump grows by.
Here is a similar one: 4, 6, 9, 13, 18. The jumps are 2, 3, 4 and 5, going up by 1. The next jump is 6, so the next number is 18 + 6 = 24.

stepByStep.text: The jumps go up by 1 each time, so the next jump is 7.
Add 7 to the last number. The next number is 28.

misconceptions.A: 25 is 21 + 4, using an old jump. The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, so the next one is bigger than 6.
misconceptions.B: Great job! The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and then 7, and 21 + 7 = 28.
misconceptions.C: 27 is 21 + 6, using the last jump again. The jumps grow by 1 each time.
misconceptions.D: 30 is 21 + 9, a jump that is too big. After a jump of 6 comes a jump of 7.

questionText: What is the next term: 2, 5, 14, 41, ______
hints: Look at the jumps between the terms. They are not steady, so see how each jump is made from the jump before it.
Work out the three jumps: from 2 to 5, from 5 to 14 and from 14 to 41. Ask yourself how many times bigger each jump is than the last.
Here is a similar one: 1, 3, 7, 15. The jumps are 2, 4 and 8, each double the one before. The next jump is 16, so the next term is 15 + 16 = 31.

stepByStep.text: Find the jumps: 5 − 2 = 3, 14 − 5 = 9 and 41 − 14 = 27.
The jumps do not grow by adding. Each jump is 3 times the one before: 3 × 3 = 9 and 9 × 3 = 27. So the next jump is 81.
Add 81 to the last term to get 122.
You can check another way. Each term is 3 times the one before, take away 1. 41 × 3 = 123 and 123 − 1 = 122, so the next term is 122.

misconceptions.A: 50 is 41 + 9, using an old jump. The jumps 3, 9 and 27 get 3 times bigger each time.
misconceptions.B: 120 is close. Find the next jump by multiplying 27 by 3, then add it to 41.
misconceptions.C: Excellent thinking! The jumps are 3, 9, 27 and then 81, and 41 + 81 = 122.
misconceptions.D: 82 is double 41. Doubling does not fit the earlier terms, because double 2 is 4 and the second term is 5.

questionText: Find the next term: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, ______
hints: The numbers grow faster and faster, so look at multiplying. See what each term is multiplied by to get the next one, and whether that multiplier changes.
Work out what 1 is multiplied by to give 2, then what 2 is multiplied by to give 6, then 6 to give 24. Look at those multipliers in order.
Here is a similar one: 4, 8, 24, 96. Here 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 3 = 24 and 24 × 4 = 96. The multiplier goes up by 1 each time, so the next term is 96 × 5 = 480.

stepByStep.text: See what each term is multiplied by to get the next: 1 × 2 = 2, 2 × 3 = 6, 6 × 4 = 24 and 24 × 5 = 120.
The multiplier goes up by 1 each time: 2, 3, 4, 5. The next multiplier is 6.
Multiply the last term by 6. The next term is 720.

misconceptions.A: 360 is 120 × 3, using an old multiplier. The multipliers go 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next one is 6.
misconceptions.B: You got it! The multipliers are 2, 3, 4, 5 and then 6, and 120 × 6 = 720.
misconceptions.C: 240 is 120 × 2, using the first multiplier again. The multipliers go 2, 3, 4, 5, so the next one is 6.
misconceptions.D: 600 is 120 × 5, using the last multiplier again. The multiplier grows by 1 each time.

questionText: Find the missing number: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ______
hints: The jumps here are not steady. Look at how each number is linked to the two numbers just before it.
Add the first two numbers, 2 and 3, and compare the total with the third number. Then try the same with 3 and 5.
Here is a similar one: 1, 4, 5, 9, 14. Each number is the sum of the two before it: 1 + 4 = 5, 4 + 5 = 9 and 5 + 9 = 14. The next number is 9 + 14 = 23.

stepByStep.text: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13 and 8 + 13 = 21.
Add the last two numbers. The missing number is 34.

misconceptions.A: Well done! Each number is the sum of the two before it, and 13 + 21 = 34.
misconceptions.B: 29 is 21 + 8, using the last jump again. Add the last two numbers of the list instead.
misconceptions.C: 26 is 21 + 5. Each number here is the sum of the two numbers before it.
misconceptions.D: 32 is close. Add 13 and 21 once more, ones first and then tens.

questionText: Which number does NOT belong: 2, 5, 10, 17, 28, 37
hints: Find the differences: 3, 5, 7, 11, 9. Most differences are odd numbers increasing by 2.
Expected differences: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. The actual sequence should be: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37.
28 should be 26. So 28 is the number that doesn't belong!

stepByStep.text: Differences: 3, 5, 7, 11, 9 — pattern breaks!
Expected: +3, +5, +7, +9, +11. Correct sequence: 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, 37
28 doesn't belong. It should be 26.

misconceptions.B: 10 fits the pattern (5+5=10)
misconceptions.C: 37 fits the corrected pattern (26+11=37)
misconceptions.D: 17 fits the pattern (10+7=17)

questionText: Find the next term: 4, 12, 36, 108, ______
hints: The numbers grow faster and faster, so adding the same amount will not fit. See what each term is multiplied by to get the next one.
Compare 4 and 12, then 12 and 36. Ask yourself how many times bigger each term is than the one before.
Here is a similar one: 2, 10, 50, 250. Each term is 5 times the one before. So the next term is 250 × 5 = 1250.

stepByStep.text: See how each term is made from the one before: 4 × 3 = 12, 12 × 3 = 36 and 36 × 3 = 108.
Each term is 3 times the one before. Multiply 108 by 3 to find that the next term is 324.

misconceptions.A: 144 is 108 + 36. This pattern multiplies each time, so multiply 108 by 3.
misconceptions.B: Great job! Each term is 3 times the one before, and 108 × 3 = 324.
misconceptions.C: 216 is 108 × 2. Check the earlier terms: 4 is multiplied by 3 to give 12, not by 2.
misconceptions.D: 432 is 108 × 4. Check the earlier terms: 4 is multiplied by 3 to give 12, not by 4.

questionText: The sequence 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42 follows the pattern n × (n+1). What is the 10th term?
hints: The rule is given to you: each term is its position number multiplied by the next counting number. You only need to use the rule for the right position.
Check the rule on a term you know. The 3rd term is 3 × 4 = 12. Now decide which two numbers to multiply for the 10th term.
Here is a similar one. With the same rule, the 7th term is 7 times the next counting number, which is 8. 7 × 8 = 56, so the 7th term is 56.

stepByStep.text: The rule says the term in position n is n times the number just after n. Check it: the 1st term is 1 × 2 = 2 and the 2nd term is 2 × 3 = 6.
For the 10th term, n is 10 and the number just after it is 11.
Multiply 10 by 11. The 10th term is 110.

misconceptions.A: Excellent thinking! The 10th term is 10 times the next number, 11, which is 110.
misconceptions.B: 90 is 9 × 10, which is the 9th term. For the 10th term, multiply 10 by the number after it.
misconceptions.C: 100 is 10 × 10. The rule multiplies 10 by the next number, which is 11.
misconceptions.D: 120 is 10 × 12. The rule uses the number just after 10, which is 11.

hints: This looks like two patterns woven together. Try reading every other number, and then the numbers in between.
Write down the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th numbers on one line. Write the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th numbers on another line and compare the two lines.
Here is a similar one: 1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 6, 4. The 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th numbers are 1, 2, 3 and 4. The number after each of them is its double: 2, 4, 6. So after the 4 comes its double, 8.

stepByStep.text: Two patterns are woven together. Take every other number, starting from the first: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. These are the counting numbers.
Now take the numbers in between: 1, 4, 9, 16. Each one is the number just before it multiplied by itself: 2 × 2 = 4, 3 × 3 = 9 and 4 × 4 = 16.
The gap comes straight after 5, so it is 5 multiplied by itself. The next term is 25.

misconceptions.A: 20 is 4 × 5. Each in-between number is the number before it multiplied by itself, so use 5 × 5.
misconceptions.B: You got it! Each in-between number is the number before it multiplied by itself, and 5 × 5 = 25.
misconceptions.C: 6 would carry on the counting numbers, but the gap belongs to the other pattern: 1, 4, 9, 16.
misconceptions.D: 10 is double 5. Look at the pairs 2 and 4, 3 and 9, 4 and 16 to see what is done to each number.
